cards.title: THE DINING ROOM
cards.tagline: ONE JOB. THE ONLY ROOM THAT CAN LOSE IT QUIETLY.
cards.objective: The dining room has one job, and it is the only room in the house that can quietly lose that job without anyone noticing. This card is the map.
cards.start_here: DRZ-001 Dining Table. Start with the Dining Table. It is the quickest zone in the room and the only one whose result shows up at dinner the same evening, which buys you the goodwill to open the sideboard drawers tomorrow.
how_to_play: 1. Deal the five ZONE cards face up. Pick the one that is annoying you today, or take the one this card says to start at.
2. Lay out that zone's three FRICTION cards. Keep the ones that are true in your dining room. Put the rest back.
3. Turn a friction card over and pick the answer that is true. It names a ROOT CAUSE.
4. The root cause card names the ACTION cards that fix that cause. Pick the one that matches the time you actually have: fifteen or thirty minutes.
5. Do it standing up, with the card in your hand.
6. Read the victory condition out loud. If it is not true yet, you are not finished, and that is the whole scoring system.
7. Fill in the zone's STANDARD card with a pen and put it where the zone is.
8. Draw an EVENT card when an ordinary hard day happens, and see whether the standard held.
cards.players: 1 to 6. With more than one, deal the friction cards out and let each person keep the ones they believe. Disagreement is the useful part, not a problem to resolve before starting.
cards.six_s: Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety, Standardize, Sustain
cards.safety_first: Do DRA-011 The Full Dining Room Safety Walk before any rebuild. It takes thirty minutes and covers every chair, the cabinet strap, and whether alcohol and candles are kept out of a child's reach.

cards.title: DINING TABLE
cards.tagline: ONE CENTERPIECE. BARE WOOD. NOTHING ELSE ON IT.
cards.objective: Seat everyone for a shared meal without having to move anything first.
callouts: One centerpiece sitting alone on bare wood
Every chair pushed fully in, nothing hanging off any chair back
No paper anywhere on the tabletop
A trivet visible just inside the nearest sideboard drawer
Placemats stacked in that same drawer
The chair rungs and legs clear of anything leaning against them
cards.done_looks_like: One centerpiece on bare wood and nothing else, every chair pushed all the way in with nothing hanging off its back, placemats and trivets in the sideboard drawer one step away, and no paper anywhere on the surface.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: Candles set at the ends of a table runner catch the runner before anyone sitting at the table notices, and a hot serving dish on bare wood scorches it and can crack a glass top.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: A drop leaf or an extension table with a worn latch can fold on a hand when someone leans on it, and dining chairs work loose at the rungs long before they actually break.

the_call.title: The person who works at the table
the_call.text: Someone in the house has made the table their desk, and every reset you have run so far has been a polite request that they stop. Requests do not hold. Here is the rule that settles it: if an activity lands on the table more than three evenings in a week, it is not clutter, it is an activity with nowhere else to be, and no table standard will survive it. Give that activity a caddy it lives in and a named shelf it goes back to, or accept that this is a desk and stop calling the room a dining room. Then decide which meal you are protecting, Sunday lunch or weeknight dinner, say it out loud to the household, and let everything outside that meal be negotiable.

cards.title: BUFFET OR SIDEBOARD SURFACE
cards.tagline: ONE BARE RUN FOR SERVING. THREE PIECES FOR DISPLAY.
cards.objective: Hold serving dishes during a meal and a small, deliberate display between them.
callouts: A strip of tape marking a bare serving run at one end of the sideboard
Three display objects grouped together at the lamp end
A lamp standing among the display objects
The lamp's cord the only cord visible
No paper anywhere on the wood
The serving run empty and clear of any object
cards.done_looks_like: A taped run of bare wood at the end nearest the table long enough for the roasting pan, three display objects grouped at the lamp end, no paper on the wood, and the lamp cord the only cord in sight.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: A sideboard often ends up carrying a lamp, a phone charger, and a warming tray on one outlet behind the furniture where you never look. Count what is on that plug and feel the strip for warmth or discoloring.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: Tall vases and heavy candlesticks on a narrow sideboard sit at head height for a small child and topple when the drawer below is yanked open.

the_call.title: The clear run you actually need
the_call.text: You have been asking one surface to do three jobs: serving, display, and mail. It cannot, and the mail always wins, because paper arrives daily and decor does not. Settle it with a measurement rather than an intention. Take the largest dish you genuinely serve from this surface, the roasting pan or the big salad bowl, set it down where you would really set it, and mark that length of wood with a strip of tape. That run is protected and nothing lives on it, ever. Now look at your decor in what is left. Whatever does not fit in the remaining length leaves the room, however much you like it, and the mail never had a claim here to begin with.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: Platters and the punch bowl stored above shoulder height come down while your arms are already loaded, and a drawer packed tight with linens can pull clean out of its runners.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: Boxes of taper candles and long matches sitting loose in a low sideboard drawer are exactly at a child's reach and open on all sides.

the_call.title: The tablecloth for a table you don't own
the_call.text: This drawer is full of linen from other houses, other tables, and other decades, and you keep it because letting go of good cloth feels wasteful. Make it a measuring problem instead of a feeling. Measure your table, then measure every cloth: one that does not hang at least a hand's depth over your actual table edge on all sides will never get used, because it looks wrong the moment it goes on and you will fold it away again. Keep the cloths that fit the table you own, plus one sized for the table with the leaf in. Anything carrying a stain you have already treated once and failed to shift becomes rags today, not next season. Partial napkin sets travel with the cloth they match, or they go with it.

cards.title: CHINA OR DISPLAY CABINET
cards.tagline: EIGHT PLATES HIGH, WITH FELT BETWEEN THEM. STRAPPED TO THE WALL.
cards.objective: Keep the good tableware safe, visible, and genuinely usable.
callouts: A stack of plates no taller than eight, felt visible between each plate
Cups standing single file in a row rather than nested together
Glasses standing rim up on a clean shelf liner
A tureen sitting on the cabinet's bottom shelf
A visible strap securing the cabinet to the wall
A small photo taped to the inside of the cabinet door
cards.done_looks_like: Plates stacked no more than eight high with felt between them, cups standing single file rather than nested, glasses rim up on a clean liner, tureens on the bottom shelf, the cabinet strapped to a wall stud, and a photo of the finished shelves taped inside the door.

safety_checks.question: Fall, cut, or crush
safety_checks.text: A tall glass-fronted cabinet loaded with heavy plates is the largest tip-over risk in this room, and its shelves make an inviting ladder for a small child.

safety_checks.question: Poison, choke, or strangle
safety_checks.text: Decorative antique and hand-painted pieces of unknown origin can carry lead in the glaze, particularly on gilt rims and bright reds. Display them, but keep acidic food and drink off them.

the_call.title: The twelve settings from your grandmother
the_call.text: This is the hardest decision in the room and everyone knows why: the china is not china, it is a person. Separate the two on purpose. Keep the number of settings that fits the largest meal you have actually hosted in the past three years, plus two for breakage. For the rest, write down whose they were and what you remember about them, photograph them alongside that note, and offer them to the relative most likely to set a table with them, then sell or donate whatever nobody claims. Then the part people skip: what you keep, you owe use. Name an occasion, once a year at minimum, when it goes on the table. China that never leaves the cabinet is not being honored. It is being stored behind glass.

cards.title: BEVERAGE OR COFFEE STATION
cards.tagline: ONE TRAY. LEFT TO RIGHT. A LINE ON THE JAR.
cards.objective: Make a drink and hand it over without crossing into the kitchen.
callouts: A coffee machine, grounds, mugs, and spoons arranged left to right on one tray
The whole arrangement sitting on a single liftable tray
A marked fill line visible on the bean jar

A hand's width of clear space behind the kettle
Spoons and sugar grouped together at one end of the tray
cards.done_looks_like: Machine, grounds, mugs, then spoons and sugar running left to right along one liftable tray, mugs capped at the number of daily drinkers plus two, a marked fill line on the bean jar, and a hand's width of clear air behind the kettle.

safety_checks.question: Water and electricity
safety_checks.text: The machine, the kettle, and an open water jug share a small surface, and cords near the front edge get hooked by a sleeve. Keep the appliances on their own outlet and never top up a plugged-in machine over its base.

safety_checks.question: Burn or fire
safety_checks.text: A kettle boiling directly under a wall shelf drives steam into the underside of it, warping the shelf and dropping condensation onto the plug below.

the_call.title: The second machine
the_call.text: There are at least two ways to make a hot drink on this counter, and one of them is kept for the person you meant to become. Do not settle it from memory, because memory is generous about the press you used enthusiastically for three weeks the summer you bought it. Put a sticky note on each machine and make a mark every time it produces a drink someone actually drinks. Give it one full week, weekend included. Any machine with fewer than three marks comes off the counter and goes into a cupboard for one more month, and if it is still unused at the end of that month it leaves the house. The same test settles the mug shelf: the mugs you reach past every single morning are not favorites, they are furniture.

cards.tagline: WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE. THEN WHY.
cards.objective: There are two ways to make a hot drink on this counter, and one of them hasn't earned its counter space in months but nobody's tested that.

branches.answer: Getting rid of a machine somebody might start using again feels premature
It's been part of the counter so long it doesn't register as extra anymore
There's no actual rule for how little use earns a machine its spot

cards.instruction: Pick the answer that is true in your dining room, then turn to that root cause card. If two are true, take the one you could change this week.

art.subject: two coffee-making machines side by side on a counter, one with a sticky note and tally marks on it, the other bare and unused beside it
must_show: There are two ways to make a hot drink on this counter, and one of them hasn't earned its counter space in months but nobody's tested that.
art.accept_test: The problem has to be visible, and it has to look like a real Tuesday rather than a disaster. A tidy picture on a friction card is a rejection: if a stranger could not say what is wrong, it failed.

cards.title: EXCESS
cards.objective: More things are kept here than the zone's job needs.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Count what you used in the past month. If the honest number is a third of what is stored here, the space is not too small.
cards.instruction: This is a Sort problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: more display objects crowded at one end of a sideboard than the space was ever meant to hold
must_show: More things are kept here than the zone's job needs.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: NO ASSIGNED HOME
cards.objective: The thing has no single defined destination, so it lands wherever the hand opens.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Ask where one specific item lives. If two people answer differently, or nobody answers, it has no home.
cards.instruction: This is a Straighten problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a stack of mail sitting on a dining table with no drawer or tray anywhere nearby assigned to catch it
must_show: The thing has no single defined destination, so it lands wherever the hand opens.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: WRONG LOCATION
cards.objective: It is stored somewhere, just not where it is used.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Stand where you use it and count the steps to where it is kept. More than two is the wrong cabinet.
cards.instruction: This is a Straighten problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a trivet sitting in a drawer at the far side of a dining room, nowhere near the table it's meant to protect
must_show: It is stored somewhere, just not where it is used.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: EXCESS MOTION
cards.objective: Getting it out means bending, lifting, unstacking, or moving something else first: too many steps.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Fetch it once and count the movements. More than two and the storage is charging you rent every time.
cards.instruction: This is a Straighten problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a stack of serving platters with the two top pieces lifted aside just to reach the one at the bottom
must_show: Getting it out means bending, lifting, unstacking, or moving something else first: too many steps.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: POOR VISIBILITY
cards.objective: You own it, but you cannot see it, so you buy it again or forget it.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Open the door and, without moving anything, name what is at the back. If you cannot, that stock is invisible.
cards.instruction: This is a Straighten problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a bean jar on a counter with its fill level impossible to see from a normal standing height
must_show: You own it, but you cannot see it, so you buy it again or forget it.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: POOR ACCESSIBILITY
cards.objective: The people who use it cannot reach it safely, or at all.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Have the shortest person who uses this zone fetch what they need daily. If they climb, reach overhead, or ask for help, the height is wrong.
cards.instruction: This is a Safety problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a heavy stoneware platter sitting on a shelf above shoulder height with no step stool anywhere nearby
must_show: The people who use it cannot reach it safely, or at all.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: INSUFFICIENT CAPACITY
cards.objective: The right storage exists and genuinely cannot hold what belongs in it.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Put back only what belongs here. If it still will not close, or still stacks four deep, the capacity is the problem, not the habit.
cards.instruction: This is a Sort problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a china cabinet shelf with plates stacked higher than the felt dividers between them were ever meant to allow
must_show: The right storage exists and genuinely cannot hold what belongs in it.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: MISSING STANDARD
cards.objective: Nobody agreed what good looks like, so everybody is right.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Ask two people in the house to describe this zone when it is finished. Two different answers means there is no standard to keep.
cards.instruction: This is a Standardize problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a sideboard surface with no taped boundary anywhere to show where serving space ends and display space begins
must_show: Nobody agreed what good looks like, so everybody is right.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: MISSING TRIGGER
cards.objective: The reset is a good intention with nothing to attach it to.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Name the moment it happens. If the answer is "when I get round to it", there is no trigger and it will not survive a bad week.
cards.instruction: This is a Sustain problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: an unlit candle burned down close to a table runner with no marked moment that would have prompted moving it sooner
must_show: The reset is a good intention with nothing to attach it to.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: SAFETY CONSTRAINT
cards.objective: The current arrangement can hurt somebody, and that outranks tidy.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Look for the four: a blade your hand would meet, weight above shoulder height, heat beside something that burns, and an unsafe placement near a child's reach.
cards.instruction: This is a Safety problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a bottle of wine standing open on a shelf at exactly the height a small child would reach
must_show: The current arrangement can hurt somebody, and that outranks tidy.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: POOR REPLENISHMENT
cards.objective: Consumables run out unnoticed, and stock ages out of use unseen.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Find the last one of something you use daily. If nothing tells you it is the last one, you will find out at the worst possible moment.
cards.instruction: This is a Standardize problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a coffee bean jar sitting visibly below its own marked fill line beside an empty mug
must_show: Consumables run out unnoticed, and stock ages out of use unseen.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: CONFLICTING USERS
cards.objective: Two people run one zone by two designs, so it is permanently half of each.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Do the shared task together, once. The argument that starts is the conflict, and it is a design problem, not a character problem.
cards.instruction: This is a Standardize problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a dining table with a laptop and papers spread across one end and a place setting arranged at the other
must_show: Two people run one zone by two designs, so it is permanently half of each.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: UNCLEAR OWNERSHIP
cards.objective: Nobody specific is responsible for resetting this zone, so upkeep depends on whoever notices first.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Ask who resets this zone. If the honest answer is "whoever gets to it" or two names with no agreement, there is no owner.
cards.instruction: This is a Sustain problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a dining chair with a visibly loose rung, standing among other chairs with nobody having marked it for repair
must_show: Nobody specific is responsible for resetting this zone, so upkeep depends on whoever notices first.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: SENTIMENTAL ATTACHMENT
cards.objective: The item is kept for what it represents, not because it is used, and the guilt stalls Sort indefinitely.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Ask if you would buy this again today for what it does. If the answer is no but you still cannot decide, the hold is sentimental.
cards.instruction: This is a Sort problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a full china cabinet of inherited place settings, far more than the table in front of it has ever been set for
must_show: The item is kept for what it represents, not because it is used, and the guilt stalls Sort indefinitely.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: UNRESOLVED DECISION
cards.objective: The item is not clutter, it is a decision that has not been made, so it is stacked instead of acted on.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Pick up one piece. If your first thought is a verb (pay, sign, call, decide) rather than a place, it needs a decision, not a home.
cards.instruction: This is a Sort problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a folded tablecloth clearly too small for the dining table it's meant to cover, kept in the drawer anyway
must_show: The item is not clutter, it is a decision that has not been made, so it is stacked instead of acted on.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: DIFFICULT TO CLEAN
cards.objective: Reaching the surface to clean it costs more effort than the rest of the zone combined, so it gets skipped.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Time how long it actually takes to reach and wipe the surface. If it requires moving something first, that cost is why it is skipped.
cards.instruction: This is a Shine problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: the dusty top of a tall china cabinet seen from below, well out of easy reach for a regular wipe
must_show: Reaching the surface to clean it costs more effort than the rest of the zone combined, so it gets skipped.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: PERCEPTUAL BLINDNESS
cards.objective: The clutter has been visible so long the eye stops flagging it as a problem.
cards.confirm_in_30_seconds: Ask someone who does not live here to name what looks out of place. If they see it instantly and you had stopped noticing, this is the cause.
cards.instruction: This is a Sort problem. Draw one of the action cards listed and do it now, at the length you actually have.

art.subject: a loose stack of mail on a sideboard that has clearly sat undisturbed long enough to look like it belongs there
must_show: The clutter has been visible so long the eye stops flagging it as a problem.
art.accept_test: One idea, one object, no room tour. If the picture could illustrate three different causes it is rejected.

cards.title: CLEAR THE TABLE BY OWNER, NOT BY TYPE
cards.objective: Clear the whole table onto the floor in one armful and sort what came off by the person it belongs to, so nothing stays homeless on a technicality.
cards.why_it_matters: A pile sorted by type just becomes three piles; sorting by owner means somebody actually carries it away.
inputs: a basket for each person's things
steps: Clear the whole table onto the floor in one armful, then sort what came off by owner rather than by type. The homework, the unopened mail, and the half-finished craft project each go back to a person, not back to the table.
Hand each pile to the person it belongs to, right now, rather than setting it back down anywhere else in the room.
Wipe the bare table once everything is off it, then set the centerpiece back down alone.
cards.victory_condition: The table holds nothing but its centerpiece, and every activity that was on it has gone home with the person who owns it.

art.subject: a dining table mid-clear with one basket holding homework and mail sitting on a chair beside it, the tabletop otherwise bare except the centerpiece going back down
must_show: The table holds nothing but its centerpiece, and every activity that was on it has gone home with the person who owns it.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: PHOTOGRAPH BOTH STATES AND TAPE THEM INSIDE THE DOOR
cards.objective: Photograph the table both set for a meal and cleared to its standard, and tape both pictures inside the sideboard door so the standard isn't something anyone has to remember.
cards.why_it_matters: A standard living only in someone's head resets differently every night; a photo taped where people can see it resets the same way every time.
steps: Set the table as if for a real meal and photograph it.
Clear it to bare wood plus the centerpiece and photograph that too.
Confirm the trivet and placemats live in the sideboard drawer nearest the table, not one further away, then tape both photos inside that door at eye level.
cards.victory_condition: Both photos are taped inside the sideboard door, and anyone in the house can point at them to say what 'cleared' actually looks like.
cards.source: hand authored, steps grounded in the Manual passes

art.subject: a hand taping two photographs, one of a set table and one of a cleared table, to the inside of a sideboard door
must_show: Both photos are taped inside the sideboard door, and anyone in the house can point at them to say what 'cleared' actually looks like.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: CLEAR THE WOOD AND GIVE EVERY PAPER A VERDICT
cards.objective: Take everything off the sideboard's wood and give every piece of paper a real verdict tonight, so nothing sits there by default.
cards.why_it_matters: Paper left 'for now' is exactly how a serving surface turns into a filing cabinet.
inputs: a folder for anything to file
steps: Take everything off the wood, including the picture frames and the candlesticks, and give every piece of paper a verdict tonight: act on it, file it, or recycle it. Burnt-down candle stubs, dried flowers, and chargers belonging to other rooms leave now.
Return chargers and stray items to the room they actually belong to.
Set only the lamp and the display group you're keeping back down at the far end.
cards.victory_condition: The wood is bare, every piece of paper has a verdict, and nothing that belongs to another room is still sitting here.

art.subject: a sideboard cleared completely to bare wood with a small stack of mail sorted into an action pile, a file pile, and a recycling pile on the floor beside it
must_show: The wood is bare, every piece of paper has a verdict, and nothing that belongs to another room is still sitting here.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: TAPE THE SERVING RUN AND CAP THE DISPLAY AT THREE
cards.objective: Mark the serving run with tape sized to your largest dish, and settle the display group at exactly three objects at the far end.
cards.why_it_matters: A run you can see is a run you'll actually keep clear; an unlimited display always grows until it swallows the space mail wants to claim.
inputs: a large serving dish to measure with
steps: Set your largest serving dish where you'd really put it and mark that length with tape.
Choose exactly three display objects for the far end and put everything else away or elsewhere.
Pull the sideboard out and trace the lamp cord to the outlet so you can actually see what else shares that plug.
cards.victory_condition: The taped run stays bare, exactly three display objects sit at the far end, and you know what else shares the lamp's outlet.
cards.source: hand authored, steps grounded in the Manual passes

art.subject: a strip of tape marking a bare serving run at one end of a sideboard, exactly three display objects grouped at the far end beside a lamp
must_show: The taped run stays bare, exactly three display objects sit at the far end, and you know what else shares the lamp's outlet.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: LAY OUT EVERY LINEN AND CHECK EVERY SET
cards.objective: Pull every tablecloth, runner, and napkin out and lay them across the table to see which sets are actually complete, so nothing partial keeps its drawer space.
cards.why_it_matters: A stained cloth or an orphaned napkin only reveals itself the night you actually need the full set.
inputs: the dining table to lay things across
steps: Pull every tablecloth, runner, and napkin out and lay them across the table so you can see which sets are actually complete. Partial napkin sets, cloths with stains you have already tried and failed to lift, and serving pieces orphaned from sets you no longer own are finished.
Roll each surviving cloth with its matching napkins inside it before it goes back.
Measure what's left against the table you actually own, including the leaf in.
cards.victory_condition: Every remaining linen set is complete, every serving piece belongs to a set you still own, and nothing carries a stain you've already failed to lift.

art.subject: tablecloths, runners, and napkins spread across a dining table, one pile of complete matched sets and a smaller pile of stained or partial linens set apart
must_show: Every remaining linen set is complete, every serving piece belongs to a set you still own, and nothing carries a stain you've already failed to lift.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: MOVE THE HEAVY PIECES DOWN AND THE CANDLES UP
cards.objective: Move the punch bowl and heavy platters to the lowest shelf, and move taper candles and matches into a latched drawer or high out of a child's reach.
cards.why_it_matters: Heavy stoneware overhead comes down while your hands are already full, and loose candles and matches in a low drawer are exactly at a small child's reach.
inputs: a latch or a high shelf
steps: Move the punch bowl and heavy stoneware platters down to the bottom shelf.
Move taper candles and matches into a latched drawer, or a shelf out of reach.
Fit a divider and stand the large platters on edge behind it, so reaching one no longer means lifting the others off first.
cards.victory_condition: The heaviest pieces sit on the bottom shelf, candles and matches are latched or out of reach, and the platters stand on edge behind a divider.
cards.source: hand authored, steps grounded in the Manual passes

art.subject: a hand moving a heavy stoneware platter down onto a sideboard's bottom shelf, a latched drawer holding taper candles visible beside it
must_show: The heaviest pieces sit on the bottom shelf, candles and matches are latched or out of reach, and the platters stand on edge behind a divider.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: SPLIT THE CHINA INTO THREE HONEST GROUPS
cards.objective: Take every piece out and split it into complete sets, chipped or crazed pieces, and lone survivors, so nothing unsafe to drink from stays in rotation.
cards.why_it_matters: A chipped rim cannot be mended and is not safe to drink from, whatever the set it came from.
steps: Take every piece out and split it into three groups: complete sets, chipped or crazed pieces, and lone survivors of sets that are long gone. A chipped rim cannot be mended and is not safe to drink from, so that whole group leaves together.
Hand-wash and dry each piece you're keeping before it goes back.
Stack plates no more than eight high with felt between them as they return.
cards.victory_condition: What's left behind the glass is complete sets and pieces without a chip or crack, nothing kept only out of habit.

art.subject: china laid out on a towel-covered table in three groups, one group of chipped pieces visibly set apart in a box
must_show: What's left behind the glass is complete sets and pieces without a chip or crack, nothing kept only out of habit.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: STRAP THE CABINET AND PHOTOGRAPH THE SHELVES
cards.objective: Strap the cabinet to a wall stud, and photograph the finished shelves to tape inside the door.
cards.why_it_matters: A tall glass-fronted case loaded with plates is this room's biggest tip-over risk, and a photo means a missing piece is found in December, not next December.
steps: Find the stud and fit a wall strap between it and the cabinet.
While you're up there, dust the top of the cabinet, high and out of easy sight, with a stool and a long-handled duster.
Photograph the finished shelves and tape that photo inside the cabinet door.
cards.victory_condition: The cabinet is strapped to a wall stud, and a photo of the finished shelves is taped inside the door.
cards.source: hand authored, steps grounded in the Manual passes

art.subject: a wall strap fitted between the back of a tall china cabinet and a wall stud, a small photograph taped to the inside of the cabinet door
must_show: The cabinet is strapped to a wall stud, and a photo of the finished shelves is taped inside the door.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: CHECK EVERY DATE AND MATCH EVERY LID
cards.objective: Check the date on every tea box, syrup bottle, and pod sleeve, and match every travel mug to its lid, so nothing past date or lidless keeps its spot.
cards.why_it_matters: A syrup you'll never use again and a mug with no lid are both taking up space the morning rush actually needs.
steps: Line up every tea box, syrup bottle, and pod sleeve and check the dates, then open the travel mugs and match them to their lids. Anything past date, any mug missing its lid, and the promotional glassware you have never once poured into are out.
Recycle or donate anything you kept only because it was a gift.
Mark today's fill line on the bean jar with tape or a permanent marker.
cards.victory_condition: Everything on the counter is in date, every travel mug has its matching lid, and no glassware sits here unused.

art.subject: tea boxes, syrup bottles, and travel mugs lined up on a counter, mugs matched to their lids, a bin bag beside expired items set apart
must_show: Everything on the counter is in date, every travel mug has its matching lid, and no glassware sits here unused.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: GIVE THE MACHINE ITS OWN OUTLET AND LOCK UP THE BOTTLES
cards.objective: Give the machine and kettle their own outlet, clear cords back from the edge, and move any wine or spirits behind a latch or high out of reach.
cards.why_it_matters: Water and electricity share this counter, and an open bottle at a child's eye level is a real hazard the kitchen version of this station wouldn't have.
inputs: a latch or a high shelf
steps: Give the machine and the kettle their own outlet where possible.
Clip cords back from the front edge where a sleeve can hook them.
Move wine and spirits behind a latch or up out of a small child's reach.
cards.victory_condition: The machine and kettle have their own outlet, no cord sits at the front edge, and any alcohol is latched or out of reach.
cards.source: hand authored, steps grounded in the Manual passes

art.subject: a coffee machine and kettle each plugged into their own outlet on a counter, cords clipped back from the front edge, a latched cabinet visible below holding bottles
must_show: The machine and kettle have their own outlet, no cord sits at the front edge, and any alcohol is latched or out of reach.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: THE FULL DINING ROOM SAFETY WALK
cards.objective: Walk every zone checking the chairs, the cabinet strap, the outlets, and anything within a small child's reach.
cards.why_it_matters: A wobbly chair, an unstrapped cabinet, and an open bottle of wine all hide until someone tests for them on purpose.
steps: Rock every chair to find a loose joint, and turn any that move to face the wall.
Confirm the china cabinet is strapped to a wall stud.
Confirm alcohol and candles are out of a small child's reach throughout the room.
cards.victory_condition: No chair wobbles unmarked, the cabinet is strapped, and nothing hazardous sits within a small child's reach.
cards.source: hand authored, steps grounded in the Manual passes

art.subject: a hand rocking a dining chair to test its joints, a strapped china cabinet and a latched cabinet visible in the background
must_show: No chair wobbles unmarked, the cabinet is strapped, and nothing hazardous sits within a small child's reach.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: THE NIGHTLY CLEAR, ONE TRIP
cards.objective: When the plates go to the sink, carry out everything else on the table and the sideboard's bare run in the same trip.
cards.why_it_matters: Nothing in this room forces its own reset, so the only thing that works is tying it to a trip that was already happening.
steps: Carry the dishes to the sink.
On the same trip, carry out anything that landed on the table or the sideboard's bare run that day.
Notice whether the table matches its taped photo.
cards.victory_condition: The table and the sideboard's bare run match their standard before the kitchen light goes off.
cards.source: hand authored, steps grounded in the Manual passes

art.subject: a hand carrying a small stack of mail and a stray craft project away from a dining table in the same trip as dinner plates heading to the sink
must_show: The table and the sideboard's bare run match their standard before the kitchen light goes off.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: THE MONTHLY LIMIT AND COUNT CHECK
cards.objective: Once a month, check the sideboard's count card, the display limit, and the bean jar's fill line against what's actually there.
cards.why_it_matters: A limit written once and never revisited stops meaning anything the first time a good deal or a gift tempts you past it.
steps: Compare the count card in the sideboard drawer against what's actually in it.
Count the display objects on the sideboard surface; correct back to three if it's crept up.
Check the bean jar's fill line is still legible and accurate.
cards.victory_condition: The count card matches the drawer, the display group is back to three, and the fill line still reads true.
cards.source: hand authored, steps grounded in the Manual passes

art.subject: a hand comparing a small card taped inside a sideboard door against tablecloths and serving pieces actually in the drawer
must_show: The count card matches the drawer, the display group is back to three, and the fill line still reads true.
art.accept_test: The picture shows the finished state the victory condition describes, not the work in progress and not a person doing it.

cards.title: DINING TABLE STANDARD
cards.tagline: WRITE IT. SIGN IT. PUT IT WHERE IT HAPPENS.
cards.objective: Bare wood plus one centerpiece between meals, and every visiting activity arrives in its own container and leaves with it.
cards.trigger: When the plates go to the sink after dinner, everything else on the table travels with them.
cards.instruction: This is a write on card. Fill it in with a pen, in your own words if the printed sentence is not yours, and put it where the zone is. A standard nobody signed is a preference.
micro_quest: Run a fingernail down the leaf seam or extension joint and clear out any crumbs hiding in the gap.
Wipe the underside lip and apron rail where hands grip to pull a chair in.
Rock each chair once and flag any joint that has started to work loose.

art.subject: a set dining table with one centerpiece on bare wood, every chair pushed fully in, and a sideboard drawer visible open nearby holding placemats and a trivet, photographed plainly with a generous area of empty calm surface across the lower half for the write on lines
must_show: the zone holding its standard
art.accept_test: The lower half of the frame must be visually quiet enough to print three blank lines over it and still read.

cards.title: BUFFET OR SIDEBOARD SURFACE STANDARD
cards.tagline: WRITE IT. SIGN IT. PUT IT WHERE IT HAPPENS.
cards.objective: The taped serving run stays bare, three display objects at the far end, and no paper on the wood at any hour.
cards.trigger: When the day's mail comes through the door, it goes straight past this surface to the chair where you actually open it.
cards.instruction: This is a write on card. Fill it in with a pen, in your own words if the printed sentence is not yours, and put it where the zone is. A standard nobody signed is a preference.
micro_quest: Lift the lamp and follow its cord the whole way to the outlet, checking for a cracked or chafed patch.
Work any fresh wax drip off the wood with a plastic card before it hardens further.
Dust behind each display object rather than around it.

art.subject: a sideboard with a taped bare wood run at one end and three display objects with a lamp grouped at the other end, no paper anywhere on the surface, photographed plainly with a generous area of empty calm surface across the lower half for the write on lines

cards.title: BUFFET OR SIDEBOARD STORAGE STANDARD
cards.tagline: WRITE IT. SIGN IT. PUT IT WHERE IT HAPPENS.
cards.objective: A written count card inside the door, linens rolled with their napkins, platters on edge, and the heavy pieces on the bottom shelf.
cards.trigger: When the tablecloth comes out of the dryer, it is rolled and returned before anything else in that load gets folded.
cards.instruction: This is a write on card. Fill it in with a pen, in your own words if the printed sentence is not yours, and put it where the zone is. A standard nobody signed is a preference.
micro_quest: Smell one rolled tablecloth as you refold it, checking for a musty note that means it needs rewashing.
Check the silver-plate serving pieces together for any spreading tarnish.
Slide the drawer fully open and check it still runs flush on its runners.

cards.title: THE UNEXPECTED DINNER GUEST
cards.objective: A guest is staying for dinner tonight, unannounced, and the table has to seat one more person in the next ten minutes.
cards.held_if: The table clears to bare wood plus centerpiece in one trip, and an extra chair and place setting go down without hunting for anything.
cards.if_it_failed: If clearing the table took more than one trip, or you had to search for a chair or a setting, the nightly clear slipped. Draw DRA-002.
cards.instruction: Do not do anything to prepare. Live the day, then read the two lines below and be honest about which one you are.
cards.source: hand authored, not in the Manual

art.subject: a dining table being reset for one more guest, an extra chair being pulled in and a place setting added quickly beside three already set
must_show: A guest is staying for dinner tonight, unannounced, and the table has to seat one more person in the next ten minutes.
art.accept_test: The pressure has to be visible in the objects. No people's faces, so the load has to be shown by what is on the surfaces and, where unavoidable, by hands and feet alone.

cards.title: THE HOLIDAY SERVING RUSH

cards.if_it_failed: If a display object had to move to fit a hot dish, the run isn't actually sized for your real serving load. Draw DRA-004.

cards.if_it_failed: If you had to hunt for a missing napkin or discover a stain mid-setup, the count card or the sort slipped. Draw DRA-005.

cards.if_it_failed: If the cabinet rocked or something shifted, the strap is missing or has failed. Draw DRA-008.

cards.if_it_failed: If the bean jar ran out or mugs ran short, the replenishment check slipped. Draw DRA-009.
